newsitem.title: FRANCE: British Airways bids for France's Air Liberte.
newsitem.headline: British Airways bids for France's Air Liberte.

text.p: British Airways launched a 25 million franc ($4.82 million) bid for insolvent French carrier Air Liberte on Monday despite reports that France was unlikely to accept a foreign bid.
The British flag carrier said it believed it could revive Air Liberte by merging it with its own French subsidiary TAT.

The two airlines, which have mostly complementary routes, would have a combined 22 percent share of the French market, which is currently dominated by Air France Europe -- the domestic arm of state carrier Air France.
Monday was the deadline for bids for Air Liberte, which went into receivership on September 26.
Jacques Maillot, president of the French travel company Nouvelles Frontieres and charter company Corsair, last week said he would bid for both Air Liberte and the airline AOM.
On Monday a company officials were not available to confirm whether Maillot had submitted a bid.
AOM, formerly Air Outre-Mer, is one of the assets of state bank Credit Lyonnais that is slated to be sold as part of a state bailout of the bank.

British Airways earlier this month appealed to Brussels to block any bid by AOM for Air Liberte, claiming it would constitute an illegal use of state aid. The Consortium de Realisation, which groups the Credit Lyonnais assets to be sold, said on Monday that AOM would not make a bid.

Virgin Atlantic chairman Richard Branson said last week he might put in an offer, but a Virgin executive told the newspaper Le Monde the group was not certain that a bid for Air Liberte was the best way to expand in France.
TAT chairman Marc Rochet told a news conference in Paris that BA's business plan for Air Liberte envisaged the preservation of 1,250 jobs out of around 2,150.
He said service on all its domestic routes, including those to the French West Indies and Reunion, would be maintained.

"We're responding to a call for offers with a solid case, a detailed analysis and projections, and we have no reason not to trust in the judgment of the Creteil commercial court," which will examine the offers, Rochet said.
Le Monde reported that Prime Minister Alain Juppe is pressing for a domestic bid for Air Liberte to establish a French rival to Air France.
Creteil Court President Dominique Leveque told Reuters the court would probably issue a statement about the bid or bids received for Air Liberte on Tuesday.
"According to the law, we have six months to study the situation. But it is clear that the company's cash position cannot hold for another six months," he said.
Rochet said a long deliberation could ruin Air Liberte. He said BA's offer was good until October 30.

Air Liberte owns around a quarter of the takeoff and landing slots at Orly, Paris' second-largest airport. It lost 650 million francs in the first nine months of 1996 and has 1.5 billion francs of debt.
Air Liberte, AOM, Eurolair, BA's TAT and other carriers have been hurt by a price war aimed at increasing market share ahead of the liberalisation of the European air market in 1997.
TAT is also unprofitable, but Rochet said he expected it to swing into profit with or without a merger with Air Liberte.

Air Liberte is owned by Groupe Rivaud, with 32.3 percent, Banque Indosuez with 13 percent, International Lease Finance Corp with 12 percent, Euralair with 10 percent, Club Mediterranee with 8.5 percent, Lyonnaise de Banque with 6.2 percent and chairman Lotfi Belhassine with six percent. ($1=5.182 French Franc)
